findings.finding: 'Store root' names two different directories in two sections, so the Testing budget check is ambiguous and can under-count the real path by about 21 characters (`\rebar-gate-snapshots`). In Root cause, 'store root (92 characters ...)' is the `gate-store` directory, and `rebar-gate-snapshots\tmp` (24) is counted separately. In Testing, the build directory adds 19 characters to `store_root` ('/tmp/t-' plus 12 hex), so there `store_root` must be the `rebar-gate-snapshots` directory. The budget check then adds 'the CI root length 92' to 'the measured overhead'. If the executor reads 92 as gate-store and the overhead as the 19 measured from rebar-gate-snapshots, the 21-character `rebar-gate-snapshots` segment is never counted. The assertion would then pass even if the real path overran.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Record the 1–2 character CI headroom explicitly and state a target margin, e.g. derive 108 from the longest event-suffix constant in code and assert the budget with at least N characters of slack.
evidence: Approach: 'root + 166 characters. The usable root before git fails rises from 54 to 93 characters, which covers both the CI test root (92)'
Testing: 'for the CI root length 92, root plus the measured overhead plus `.tickets-tracker` plus a 108-character relative path is at most 259'
findings.finding: The CI path budget has 1–2 characters of headroom, and the planned budget test cannot detect erosion of that headroom. By the plan's own numbers, 92 + 166 = 258 against a 259 limit. The CI root includes variable segments (`pytest-0`, `popen-gw3`) that grow by one character at `pytest-10` or `popen-gw10`. The budget test hardcodes both 92 and 108, so it is arithmetic over constants rather than a measurement of the actual basetemp or the longest event-file name. A longer runner basetemp or a longer event suffix would pass POSIX `make verify` and fail only in the advisory post-merge sweep.
findings.location: Approach bullet 2 ('covers both the CI test root (92)'); Testing bullet 2 (budget check)
scenarios: The sweep runs with more xdist workers (popen-gw10+) or a second pytest session (pytest-1 → pytest-10): the root becomes 93 and the worst-case file fails again.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the effective usable-root limit on default Windows (published path, LongPathsEnabled off), say whether any git or Python read touches the published directory, and record the residual limit on the ticket.
evidence: Context: 'This is a product defect that affects real Windows users, not only tests'
Approach: 'The usable root before git fails rises from 54 to 93 characters'
Approach: 'Python reads of it work on the runner, where the image sets the `LongPathsEnabled` registry key (actions/runner-images#1052).'
findings.finding: The Context frames this as a defect for real Windows users, but the gain is computed only for the git-written build path. Assuming the published entry sits beside `tmp` under `rebar-gate-snapshots`, the published path is longer than the new build path. The 48-character `tickets-<40hex>` vs 14 characters gives roughly root + 196 for the worst-case file. Reading it relies on the `LongPathsEnabled` registry key, which the plan confirms only for the GitHub runner image. That key is off by default on user machines, where Python reads of published snapshot files fail once the root exceeds about 63 characters, not the claimed 93. The 'usable root rises from 54 to 93' claim therefore holds only where LongPathsEnabled is set. The plan does not say whether the donor delta path or any later git operation runs against the published directory, which would hit the same limit.
findings.location: Context / Problem ('affects real Windows users') vs Approach bullets 2–3 ('usable root ... rises from 54 to 93'; 'Python reads of it work on the runner, where the image sets the LongPathsEnabled registry key')
scenarios: A user without LongPathsEnabled and with a store root of about 70–90 characters: git materialization now succeeds, but reading the published snapshot fails with a path-too-long error.

evidence: 'Python reads of it work on the runner, where the image sets the `LongPathsEnabled` registry key (actions/runner-images#1052).'
'This is a product defect that affects real Windows users, not only tests'

'The usable root before git fails rises from 54 to 93 characters' — computed for the build path only; the published path adds `rebar-gate-snapshots\tickets-<40hex>` (21+49) versus `rebar-gate-snapshots\tmp\t-<hex12>` (25+15).
Platform fact: without the `LongPathsEnabled` registry key, Win32 file APIs (and therefore Python `open`/`stat`) reject paths longer than 259 characters, even for a long-path-aware python.exe.
findings.finding: The MAX_PATH budget analyses only the git-written build path (`store\tmp\t-<hex12>\...`, root + 166). After `os.rename` the same files live under the published entry `store\tickets-<40hex>\...`. The published entry name (48 characters, one level up) is about 30 characters longer than `tmp\t-<hex12>` (18 characters), so published file paths are about root + 196. The plan explicitly relies on the runner image's `LongPathsEnabled` registry key for Python reads of the published entry. That key is off by default on Windows 10/11 workstations and on Windows runners of other CI providers. On those hosts the binding constraint is published-path reads, which need root <= 63, not git writes, which need root <= 93. The CI test root itself (91-92) exceeds 63.
findings.location: Approach — 'The published entry name (`tickets-<40-hex sha>`, `:617`) is unchanged ... Python reads of it work on the runner, where the image sets the `LongPathsEnabled` registry key'

The defect moves from build time to read time instead of being fixed.

Windows runner on GitLab CI or Jenkins (no `LongPathsEnabled` image setting) running the same test suite at a ~92-character pytest basetemp. The 203 tests still fail, on the read of the published entry.
findings.suggested_fix: Add a 'Published path' line to the budget analysis: root + 21 + 49 + 17 + 109 = root + 196, so root <= 63 without `LongPathsEnabled`. Add the published-path arithmetic to `test_snapshot_build_dir_length.py`.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Confirm `LongPathsEnabled=1` on the `windows-latest` runner from an authoritative source (runner-images image docs or build script, or a recorded `reg query` / Python `open()` on a >260-char path in a prior sweep log) instead of citing bug report #1052, and extend the Testing budget check to cover the published `tickets-<40hex>` path, or state that the published path's MAX_PATH margin depends on that key.
evidence: Plan text: "Python reads of it work on the runner, where the image sets the `LongPathsEnabled` registry key (actions/runner-images#1052)."

Retrieved search result for https://github.com/actions/runner-images/issues/1052 is titled 'MAX_PATH lengths on Windows environment' and reads 'Describe the bug I'm hitting the MAX_PATH restriction on a windows environment...'. That is a bug report and does not confirm the key is set.
A targeted search for the runner-images build script setting `LongPathsEnabled` returned no confirming source.

Arithmetic from the plan's own components: root 92 + `\rebar-gate-snapshots\tickets-<40hex>` 70 + `\.tickets-tracker` 17 + ticket directory 20 + event file 76 ≈ 275 > 259. The plan's budget check covers only the git-written build path (root + `tmp` build + tracker + 108).
findings.finding: The plan's claim that Python can read the published entry on the runner rests on the image setting `LongPathsEnabled`, with actions/runner-images#1052 as the source, and that claim is not verified. The search result for #1052 is a bug report about hitting MAX_PATH on the Windows image, not a statement that the image enables long paths. The claim matters because, by the plan's own component lengths, the published path in CI is about 275 characters, over 259. If the key is not set, the 203 un-deselected tests still fail when they read from the published entry, and the fix will not turn the sweep green.
findings.location: Approach — bullet 'The published entry name (`tickets-<40-hex sha>`, `:617`) is unchanged ... Python reads of it work on the runner, where the image sets the `LongPathsEnabled` registry key (actions/runner-images#1052)'; Testing — 'Budget check'
scenarios: After merge the sweep runs again. The `checkout-index` builds now succeed, but if `LongPathsEnabled` is 0, Python opening `...\tickets-<40hex>\.tickets-tracker\<ticket>\<event>-REVIEW_RESULT.json` raises a path-too-long `FileNotFoundError`/`OSError`, and the removed tests fail for a different reason.
Windows users with a long store root and no `LongPathsEnabled` hit the same failure on the published path, even though the build path is now under the limit.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the #1052 citation with evidence that settles the claim: either a link to the runner-images Windows image source or readme that sets `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem\LongPathsEnabled`, or a run or job id where a step ran `reg query HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\FileSystem /v LongPathsEnabled` and showed 0x1. In Testing, add a second budget assertion or note: published path = root + len('/rebar-gate-snapshots/tickets-') + 40 + `.tickets-tracker` + 108. That is over 259 at the CI root of 92 and depends on `LongPathsEnabled`, but at a typical user root of about 45 it is about 235 and fits under MAX_PATH.

findings.finding: Handling of the 13 `test_autodeploy_prune.py` deselects depends on a sibling change (citreous-talented-wildebeest's Gerrit 3428), but no dependency edge is declared and this ticket has no clear closure condition. The plan also asserts, without verification, that the `requires_posix_shell` skip ('where /bin/sh is absent') will fire on the runner. evidence: 'for the CI root length 92 ... plus a 108-character relative path is at most 259'
'The usable root before git fails rises from 54 to 93 characters, which covers both the CI test root (92)'

Counting the example root `C:\Users\runneradmin\AppData\Local\Temp\pytest-of-runneradmin\pytest-0\popen-gw3\gate-store` gives 91 characters; 91 + 5 separators + 24 + 53 + 16 + 19 + 75 = 283, so '92' is off by one (or includes a separator).
findings.finding: The budget check is arithmetic on hard-coded literals: CI root 92 and worst-case relative path 108. So it cannot detect a regression caused by a new, longer event-file suffix, or by a longer root. It also has only 1-2 characters of headroom against the plan's own threshold. Usable root is 93, CI root is stated as 92, and the example path's root actually counts 91 characters. Any growth re-breaks the sweep without the test noticing, for example `popen-gw10` on a larger runner, an `.args`-unrelated basetemp change, or a new event type whose suffix exceeds `COMPLETION_VERDICT.json.retired`.
findings.location: Testing — 'Budget check (edge: the worst-case file): for the CI root length 92, root plus the measured overhead plus `.tickets-tracker` plus a 108-character relative path is at most 259.'
scenarios: A new ticket event type with a longer suffix than `COMPLETION_VERDICT.json.retired` lands. The literal 108 still passes the budget test, but Windows sweeps fail again.
The sweep runs with more xdist workers (`popen-gw10`) or a deeper basetemp, and the 1-2 character margin is consumed.
findings.suggested_fix: In the budget test, compute the longest relative path as len(ticket_id) + 1 + len(timestamp) + 1 + 36 + 1 + max(len(suffix) for suffix in the event-type registry) + len('.retired'), and assert root + overhead + that value <= 259. Record the headroom in the ticket so a future suffix addition is a visible budget decision.

delta_tree._link_tree_paths opens files in the published donor tree via Python os.link. That is fine with LongPathsEnabled, but it confirms that published long paths really are read after the fix.
Evidence class: Partially-verified. The registry key is cited from an issue, not observed in any run of this workflow, and the measured failures stop before any published-entry read.
findings.finding: Only the build directory is shortened. The published entry keeps `tickets-<40-hex sha>`, so in the CI test root a published ticket file is still over MAX_PATH. Using the plan's own components: 92 (root) + 1 + 20 (`rebar-gate-snapshots`) + 1 + 48 (`tickets-<sha40>`) + 1 + 16 (`.tickets-tracker`) + 1 + 95 (the example ticket dir and event file) = 275 characters. With the 108-character worst case it is 288. Every read of a published entry after the rename therefore depends on a Windows capability the plan asserts but has not observed: the runner image's LongPathsEnabled key (actions/runner-images#1052) together with a long-path-aware python.exe. It also depends on no non-Python consumer, such as git or a subprocess tool, opening those paths. Evidence class: Partially-verified. The sweep runs measured so far all failed earlier, at checkout-index, so no Windows run has yet read a published entry longer than 260 characters.
findings.location: Approach — 'The published entry name ... Python reads of it work on the runner, where the image sets the LongPathsEnabled registry key (actions/runner-images#1052)'
scenarios: After merge, a removed test fails at a later step, reading a published entry with Python or a tool, because the long-path behaviour differs from what the plan assumed. The failure is the same MAX_PATH class, so the plan's 'different cause' fallback does not clearly apply, and the ticket stalls.

Real Windows users without LongPathsEnabled who have a long store root can hit the same limit on published paths. That contradicts the product-defect framing, which only budgets for the git-written build path.
findings.suggested_fix: Add one sentence to Approach: the published-entry path in the CI root is about 275-288 characters, so reads after the rename depend on LongPathsEnabled plus the long-path-aware python.exe manifest, and no git or other subprocess reads published entries. Add one line to the post-merge plan: if a removed test fails on a published-entry path, that counts as this class (not a 'different cause'). The node id goes back into max-path.args, and a follow-up shortens or budgets the published name.
